analysis.one_liner: Taxes big investment gains at normal income rates and ends the step-up that erases gains at death.
analysis.headline: Introduced in March 2026 with three cosponsors, the Equal Tax Act has sat in the Senate Finance Committee with no hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Today, gains from selling stocks and other investments are taxed at lower rates than wages, and when someone dies holding appreciated assets, the gain is never taxed at all — heirs inherit the property at its current value. This bill would keep the lower rate only for households whose total income is $1 million or less, tax gains above that like regular income, and treat assets given away or left at death as if they were sold, so the gain is finally taxed. It shields the first $1 million of gain at death, gives family farms and family businesses a 50 percent break on gains above that, allows estates to pay over five years at a reduced interest rate, and caps two loopholes: the real-estate 'like-kind exchange' and the deduction for business owners' pass-through income.
analysis.who_benefits: Households earning under $1 million, who would never face the new rules, and who could benefit if the added revenue is used to lower deficits or fund programs; the tax code would stop rewarding income from wealth over income from work at the top.

how_it_helps.text: Keeps the preferential capital gains and dividend rate only for taxpayers whose total income does not exceed $1 million; gains above that line are taxed at ordinary income rates [S2].
Treats property transferred by gift or at death as sold for fair market value, closing the rule under which appreciated assets passed to heirs trigger no tax on the gain [S2].

Excludes the first $1 million of gain from transfers at death, and exempts 50 percent of gains above that for qualifying family farms and family businesses that commit to keeping the property in farm or business use for 10 years [S2].
Caps the like-kind exchange deferral for real estate at $500,000 per year and $1 million over a lifetime, while fully preserving it for farmland and same-purpose exchanges [S2].
Limits the qualified business income deduction to taxpayers with taxable income of $1 million or less and stops capital gains from counting toward it [S2].

analysis.who_pays: The wealthiest households — those realizing more than $1 million in gains, heirs of large estates, large real-estate investors using tax-deferred exchanges, and high-income owners of pass-through businesses. Wealth advisers and tax-preparation services would also take on heavier compliance work.

drawbacks.text: Valuing illiquid assets — a closely held business, artwork, land — at death or gift is factually difficult and would create disputes, valuations, and compliance costs for estates and the IRS; the bill adds new information returns for gifts and bequests to manage this [S2].

The bill carves out new preferences of its own: a $1 million exclusion at death, a 50 percent farm and family business break, and a five-year installment plan at 45 percent of the normal interest rate, softening the tax for the very estates it targets and adding complexity [S2].

Critics of taxing gains at death argue it can force heirs to sell assets to pay the tax; the bill's own structure — the $1 million exclusion, farm and business carve-outs, and installment option — is a response to that objection [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core change is targeted: households under $1 million in income pay nothing more, and the bill builds in protection for family farms and businesses and installment payment for estates. The real costs are administrative — valuing assets at death is genuinely hard, and the layered carve-outs make the code more complicated. On balance, a straightforward attempt to make a dollar of investment gains above $1 million taxed like a dollar of wages, with the usual costs of policing complex wealth.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it has sat without a hearing, markup, or vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Markey introduced the bill on March 17, 2026, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance [S1][S4].
Three senators cosponsored it: Sens. Sanders (I-VT), Merkley (D-OR), and Booker (D-NJ) [S3].
No further action — no committee markup, hearing, or floor vote — appears in the action history after the referral [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Wealthy households, large real-estate investors, and their heirs, who keep the stepped-up basis at death and unlimited exchange deferrals because the bill has not advanced. Short: 'Wealthy households and large investors, for now'.

for.name: Sen. Edward Markey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Senate Finance Committee.

for.name: Sens. Jeff Merkley and Cory Booker

against.name: Sen. Mike Crapo
against.what_they_did: Has not scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill since its referral to his committee.

against.name: Sen. John Thune
against.what_they_did: Controls the Senate floor schedule and has not brought the bill up for a vote.

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors are Democrats or independents; Republicans hold 55 of 100 Senate seats and no Republican has supported the bill, and no recorded opposition vote exists because it has not reached one.

industries.industry: Wealthiest households and large investment holders
industries.note: Gains above $1 million would be taxed at ordinary rates, and appreciated assets given away or left at death would be treated as sold, ending the rule under which unrealized gains can pass untaxed to heirs. These are the households that currently benefit most from the preferential rate.

The like-kind exchange, which defers tax on real-estate gains indefinitely by rolling them into new properties, would be capped at $500,000 per year and $1 million per lifetime. Investors who built wealth through repeated tax-deferred swaps would pay sooner.

The 20 percent qualified business income deduction would be unavailable to taxpayers with more than $1 million in taxable income, raising taxes on high-earning owners of partnerships and S corporations.

industries.industry: Family farms and small family businesses
industries.note: The deemed-realization rule reaches them, but they get 50 percent of gains above $1 million excluded at death and a full carve-out from the like-kind exchange cap, if they keep the property in farm or business use for ten years. Ordinary family operations are largely shielded.

industries.industry: Wealth management, trust, and tax-preparation services
industries.note: Valuation at death, new gift reporting, and trust rules would add compliance work — new billable complexity — while closing the buy-borrow-die and exchange strategies many firms advise on.

analysis.trajectory: With Republicans holding 55 Senate seats and the bill referred to the Finance Committee without a hearing, it is unlikely to advance this Congress; single-sponsor tax rewrites of this kind typically die in committee.
